newsitem.title: UK: OVERNIGHT-PARIS STOCKS SOAR DESPITE FRENCH LEFT WIN.
newsitem.headline: OVERNIGHT-PARIS STOCKS SOAR DESPITE FRENCH LEFT WIN.

text.p: A roller-coaster Paris bourse left behind early heavy losses to soar by two percent on Monday with investors betting that the new socialist-led government would not adopt market-unfriendly policies.
In currency markets, the dollar climbed by two pfennigs as the shock left-wing victory in the French parliamentary elections sent players scurrying into safe-haven currencies.

Elsewhere in Europe, Frankfurt stocks ended with healthy gains, with the export sector boosted by the stronger dollar, but London shares were well down, hit by profit-taking in a volatile financial sector.

All eyes were on the French markets where the bourse swung from minus three percent to plus two percent as investors initially took fright at the left's victory, then decided to give them the benefit of the doubt.

The blue-chip CAC-40 index plummeted 85.19 points to 2,498.75 within minutes of the opening as markets digested a "worst case scenario" for French markets in which the Socialist-led left would need the communists to form a government.

But the market recovered its nerve and was up to 3,608.61 by midafternoon in heavy trading, though some of these gains were later eroded. Dollar-earning sectors boomed but stocks involved in privatisations and restructurings suffered.

"People aren't that scared," one trader said. "They can't raise taxes. The right already did that. They can make life miserable for companies trying to restructure but they can't stop that. They'll do symbolic things."

The bourse, which fell 6.48 percent last week in the run-up to Sunday's poll, was expected to stay volatile ahead of an announcement by the new government on its policies and composition. Conglomerate Lagardere , down 7.6
percent, and defence electronics firm Thomson-CSF, down 6.9 percent, were the top CAC losers as privatisation stocks were the hardest hit in early trade.
In Frankfurt, floor trade finished with gains of 1.6 percent, shaking off worries about the future of currency union and the row between Germany and the Bundesbank about assets revaluation.
In after-hours trading on the computerised IBIS index, stocks climbed, helped partly by the stronger dollar, which improved prospects for exports.
In London by contrast, shares were down 0.84 percent, tracking a volatile bank sector as profit-taking followed the long-awaited debut as a bank of the former mutual Halifax Plc .

Dealers said the French poll result had added to uncertainties over prospects for European monetary union, adding that an expected rise in British interest rates later this week created an uncertain prospect for shares

"The market was met by a successful Halifax debut, which helped us at the open. But people pulled back, took profits in the banks, and paused to re-assess," said one senior dealer. A negative start on Wall Street did nothing to help.
In currency markets, the dollar could do no wrong amid renewed uncertainty about the single European currency.

With the French Socialists reliant on the Communists to form a government and pledging a Europe without austerity, analysts said the market was now fretting that this meant either delay or a broad-based, soft euro.
"Neither of those will be palatable to the European bloc -- near-term it seems the dollar is the winner," said Adam Chester, international bond strategist at Yamaichi International.
The dollar romped to 1.7257 marks up two pfennigs on the levels of seen in late Europe. Against the French franc, it jumped to near one-month peaks of 5.8302 compared to 5.7705 on Friday.

Fears of a broad, weak European single currency were fuelled by French Socialist spokesman Francois Hollande, who called for Italy and Spain to be included in EMU and said all stood to benefit if the euro "no longer means austerity".

"The French election results have increased the prospect of a softer euro. That is clearly bad news for the deutschmark, and clearly the dollar has benefited," said Nick Stamenkovic, economist at DKB International here.
Analysts said the U.S. curency was set to remain the darling of currency markets after France's left-wing win.
